title: Factor an injective fs chart through free generators and a group-isomorphism chart
statement:
Let $P,Q$ be fine saturated commutative monoids [def-trf-fs-log-blowup], written additively, and let $g:P\to Q$ be a homomorphism for which $g^{\rm gp}:P^{\rm gp}\to Q^{\rm gp}$ is injective. Suppose its cokernel $L=Q^{\rm gp}/g^{\rm gp}(P^{\rm gp})$ is torsion free, meaning $n\ell=0$, $n>0$, implies $\ell=0$. Then there exist an integer $r\geq0$ and elements $q_1,\ldots,q_r\in Q$ whose images form a $\mathbf Z$-basis of $L$. In particular the homomorphism
$$h:P\oplus\mathbf N^r\longrightarrow Q,\qquad (p,(n_i))\longmapsto g(p)+\sum_i n_iq_i$$
is injective and $h^{\rm gp}:P^{\rm gp}\oplus\mathbf Z^r\to Q^{\rm gp}$ is an isomorphism. The direct sum here is the Cartesian product with componentwise addition, and a $\mathbf Z$-basis means that every element has a unique expression as an integer linear combination. The empty basis is allowed when $r=0$.

source.place: Expose VI, Proposition 1.9 proof, printed p. 71, the injective monoid chart with free cokernel; Expose VIII, 3.1.1--3.1.2 and 3.1.9--3.1.10, printed pp. 98--99, for sharpening, localization and finite saturated monoids. The free-generator factorization is an agent-supplied algebraic refinement; its argument is recorded in report.md, not attributed verbatim to ILO.

proof.text: Put $G=Q^{\rm gp}$, $H=g^{\rm gp}(P^{\rm gp})$, and let $\pi:G\to L=G/H$ be the quotient. Identify $P,Q$ with their images in their group completions, as permitted by integrality in [def-trf-fs-log-blowup]. Set $S=\pi(Q)\subseteq L$. Choose finitely many monoid generators of $Q$; their images generate $S$ as a monoid and $L$ as a group, because every element of $G$ is a difference of elements of $Q$. Thus $L$ is a finitely generated abelian group. It is torsion free by hypothesis, so [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free] supplies a finite $\mathbf Z$-basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$. Use its coordinates to identify $L$ with $\mathbf Z^r$.

source.place: VI 3.7(a), printed p. 75, finite basis for a finitely generated torsion-free group; agent-supplied application to the cokernel of the chart of VI 1.9.

proof.text:
The image monoid $S$ is saturated in $L$. Indeed, suppose $n\ell\in S$ with $n\geq1$. Choose $x\in G$ lifting $\ell$ and $q\in Q$ with $\pi(q)=n\ell$. Since $nx-q\in H$, there exist $a,b\in P$ with $nx=q+g(a)-g(b)$. Consequently
$$n(x+g(b))=q+g(a)+(n-1)g(b)\in Q.$$
Saturation of $Q$ in $G$ [def-trf-fs-log-blowup] gives $x+g(b)\in Q$. Its image is $\ell$, proving $\ell\in S$. This calculation uses no assumption that $g(P)$ is a face and no torsion-freeness of $G$.

source.place: VIII 3.1.17, printed p. 101, saturation convention; explicit quotient-image calculation supplied by the agent.

proof.text:
If $r=0$, $L=0$ and its empty basis already lies in $S$; proceed to Step 8. Suppose $r>0$. Let $s_1,\ldots,s_m$ be the chosen generators of $S$ and let $B$ be the $r\times m$ integer matrix of their coordinates. Since they generate $L$ as a group, express each $e_j$ as an integer combination of the $s_i$. These expressions give an $m\times r$ integer matrix $C$ with $BC=I_r$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet]:
$$1=\det(BC)=\sum_{|T|=r}\det(B^T)\det(C_T).$$
Here $\det I_r=1$ follows directly from [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Some summand is nonzero, so some ordered $r$-tuple of elements of $S$ has nonzero integer determinant. This also shows $m\geq r$, since otherwise the sum would be empty.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, applied to the integer factorization BC=I; identity determinant from the Leibniz formula.

proof.text: Among all integer matrices whose $r$ columns belong to $S$ and whose determinant is nonzero, choose $A$ for which $D=|\det A|$ is least. Step 3 makes this set nonempty; its absolute determinants are positive integers, so the well-ordering of $\mathbf N$ supplies the least one. Determinants are integers by the finite sum of signed products in [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Write $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in S$ for the columns of $A$.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, determinant convention; agent-supplied least-positive-determinant argument.

proof.text:
By [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-adjugate-identity] over $\mathbf Q$, the matrix $A$ has inverse $\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$. In particular its columns are independent and every rational vector has unique rational coordinates in these columns. If their integer span were a proper subgroup of $\mathbf Z^r$, choose $y\in\mathbf Z^r$ outside it. Put $b=A^{-1}y\in\mathbf Q^r$, let $z_i=\lfloor b_i\rfloor\in\mathbf Z$ (the unique integer with $z_i\leq b_i<z_i+1$), and set
$$a_i=b_i-z_i,\qquad x=y-Az=Aa\in\mathbf Z^r.$$
Thus $0\leq a_i<1$. Not all $a_i$ vanish, since otherwise $y=Az$ would be in the integer span. Choose $j$ with $0<a_j<1$. These formulas explicitly produce the lattice point; no fundamental-domain theorem is being assumed.

source.place: Tag 07DQ, lemma-matrix-left-inverse, proof (adjugate identity); the rational-coordinate floor calculation is supplied explicitly by the agent.

proof.text:
Choose a positive common denominator $N$ of the finitely many rational numbers $a_i$. Then $Na_i\in\mathbf N$ and
$$Nx=\sum_i(Na_i)v_i\in S.$$
The saturation proved in Step 2 gives $x\in S$. Let $E$ be the rational identity matrix with column $j$ replaced by the vector $a$. Then $AE$ is $A$ with column $j$ replaced by $x$. The square case of [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] gives $\det(AE)=\det A\det E$. In the Leibniz sum [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] for $E$, all columns except $j$ force the permutation to fix their indices, hence also $j$; the only surviving term is $a_j$. Therefore
$$0<|\det(AE)|=a_jD<D.$$
The matrix $AE$ has integer entries (its columns are $v_i$ and $x$), and all its columns belong to $S$. This contradicts the minimality of $D$. Thus the proper-span alternative of Step 5 is impossible.

source.place: Tag 0F0K, item-cauchy-binet, square case; the column replacement determinant is computed from the Leibniz formula.

proof.text: Consequently the $v_i$ generate $\mathbf Z^r$ over $\mathbf Z$. They are independent by Step 5, so every element has a unique integer expression in the $v_i$. They are therefore a $\mathbf Z$-basis of $L$ lying in $S$. For each $i$ choose $q_i\in Q$ with $\pi(q_i)=v_i$, which is possible by the definition $S=\pi(Q)$. In rank zero make no choices. This proves the asserted basis-lifting clause.

source.place: Agent-supplied basis-lifting refinement of the injective chart with free cokernel in VI Proposition 1.9, printed p. 71.

proof.text:
Define the group homomorphism
$$\Phi:P^{\rm gp}\oplus\mathbf Z^r\to Q^{\rm gp},\qquad(u,(m_i))\mapsto g^{\rm gp}(u)+\sum_i m_iq_i.$$
If $\Phi(u,m)=0$, applying $\pi$ and using uniqueness of the basis coordinates gives $m=0$; injectivity of $g^{\rm gp}$ then gives $u=0$. Conversely, for $t\in Q^{\rm gp}$, write $\pi(t)=\sum_i m_i v_i$. Then $t-\sum_i m_iq_i\in H$, so it equals $g^{\rm gp}(u)$ for some $u$. This proves surjectivity and hence that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. If $r=0$, the same argument says precisely that $g^{\rm gp}$ is an isomorphism, since its cokernel is zero.

source.place: VI Proposition 1.9, printed p. 71, free-cokernel chart; explicit group calculation supplied by the agent.

proof.text: Restrict $\Phi$ to $P\oplus\mathbf N^r$. Its values lie in $Q$, because $g(p)$ and all $q_i$ lie there and the coefficients are nonnegative. The result is exactly $h$ in the statement, and its restriction along $p\mapsto(p,0)$ is $g$. The inclusions $P\hookrightarrow P^{\rm gp}$ and $Q\hookrightarrow Q^{\rm gp}$ are injective by integrality [def-trf-fs-log-blowup], as is $\mathbf N^r\hookrightarrow\mathbf Z^r$. Hence equality of two $h$-values gives equality of their $\Phi$-values and then equality of the inputs, proving that $h$ is injective. Group completion of the product $P\oplus\mathbf N^r$ is $P^{\rm gp}\oplus\mathbf Z^r$: a homomorphism from the product into an abelian group is uniquely the sum of its restrictions to $P$ and the $r$ coordinate generators, with the former extending to $P^{\rm gp}$ and each latter generator allowing integer multiples. Under this identification, the induced $h^{\rm gp}$ is $\Phi$, already proved an isomorphism.

source.place: VI 1.9 and VIII 3.1.1, group completions; the product universal property is checked directly.
